opus-5.5.text:
I don't think it will be a single moment where one day programmers are gone. It will be more gradual, and uneven.

First, the most well-defined, verifiable tasks go: writing a function to a clear spec, fixing a bug with a reproducible test, migrating code from one framework to another. Coding is special because it has a natural feedback signal. You can run the code and the tests and see whether it works. That makes it one of the easiest domains for reinforcement learning, so models will improve there faster than almost anywhere else.

Then the unit of work gets bigger. Today a model helps you complete a line or a file. Next it handles a whole pull request, then a feature, then maybe a small project end to end, working for hours on its own. The human role shifts from writing code to specifying what you want, reviewing, and deciding what's worth building.

So I'd say "replacement" isn't quite the right word. The activity of typing code gets replaced, but the job of a software engineer gets redefined. The bottleneck moves to taste: knowing what problem to solve, what a good product feels like, how to break an ambiguous goal into something verifiable. Those are harder for models because there's no clean reward signal.

There will be real disruption, though. If one person with a few agents can do what a team of ten did, the demand for some kinds of junior, execution-heavy work will shrink, and I don't think we should pretend otherwise. But historically, when something gets much cheaper, we use far more of it. Software that was never worth writing becomes worth writing. So I expect many more people creating software, and fewer people whose job is purely translating specs into code.

Personally, I find that exciting. Programming was always a means to an end, a way to make an idea real. If the means gets cheaper, more ideas get made real.

r001.rationale: The response says replacement will not happen all at once and describes it as gradual and uneven.

r002.rationale: It says one person with agents could do work once done by a team of ten, but does not characterize AI as concentrating power in a small number of people.

r003.rationale: It predicts reduced demand for some junior, execution-heavy work, but does not say most people will lose their distinctive value.

r004.rationale: The response gives no estimate that roughly one-thousandth of the workforce could do all the work currently done by software engineers.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think it unfolds as "replacement" in the clean sense people imagine, where one day the programmer walks out and the model walks in. It unfolds as a shift in what the job is.

Look at what's already happened. Two years ago the useful unit of work for a model was a function. Then it became a file, then a pull request, and now you can hand an agent a vague issue and it goes off for an hour, reads the codebase, runs tests, fixes its own mistakes, and comes back with something that mostly works. That trajectory matters more than any single benchmark. The thing that's getting automated isn't "programming" as an abstract skill, it's the long chain of small decisions between an intent and working code.

So what's left for the human? I'd say three things, at least for a while. First, deciding what to build and why. Models are still bad at knowing which problem is worth solving. Second, taste and judgment about systems. Is this architecture going to hurt us in six months? Is this abstraction right? Agents can propose, but someone has to own the consequences. Third, and this is the one people underestimate, verification. When an agent can write ten thousand lines in an afternoon, the bottleneck moves entirely to "how do I know this is correct?" Writing good tests, good evals, good specifications becomes the actual craft.

I think of it a bit like how reinforcement learning changed when environments got cheap. Once you can generate experience at scale, the scarce resource is no longer the policy, it's the reward signal. Programming is going through the same thing. Generating code is becoming cheap. Specifying and checking what you actually want is becoming the expensive, high-leverage part.

Where I'd push back on the optimistic framing is the middle of the distribution. Senior people get more powerful because they can direct ten agents at once. Very junior people may actually be fine, because they're cheap and learn fast. The uncomfortable squeeze is on the person whose main value was reliably turning a clear spec into clean code, because that's exactly the task that's been solved. And the training pipeline that produced seniors, where you spend years doing that work, might break. That's a real problem the industry hasn't thought hard about.

Timeline-wise, I'd avoid putting a year on it. But I'd say this: anyone who identifies as "someone who writes code" should start identifying as "someone who makes correct software happen," and start practicing with agents now, because the people who learn to supervise well will be the ones defining what the job becomes.

r001.rationale: It describes a progression from models handling functions to files, pull requests, and longer agent tasks, framing replacement as a shift in the job rather than a sudden handoff.

r002.rationale: It says senior people can become more powerful by directing multiple agents, but does not say AI will concentrate power in a small number of people.

r003.rationale: It predicts a squeeze on people whose main value is turning clear specifications into clean code, but does not claim most people will lose their distinctive value.

r004.rationale: It gives no estimate that roughly one-thousandth of the current workforce could do all of its work.

astra-6.text:
I think it will happen task by task, rather than through a single moment when AI replaces programmers. Programming includes understanding what someone wants, deciding how to build it, writing code, testing it, and maintaining it. Writing code is only one part, and it’s often the part where the objective is easiest to specify and the result easiest to check.

So I would expect AI to take over more well-defined tasks first. The harder step is giving it an ambiguous request and having it work out the requirements, navigate an existing system, and reliably deliver something useful. As that improves, a programmer’s role may shift toward deciding what to build and judging whether the result is right.

But automating more programming doesn’t necessarily mean demand for programmers falls at the same rate. If software becomes much cheaper to produce, people may build things they previously couldn’t justify building. A small team might do what once required a large team, while many more small teams become possible.

The key question, to me, is how long an AI can work independently before a person needs to intervene. Completing a function is one thing; owning a project over weeks or months is another. I’d expect the effects on jobs to become much stronger as that period of reliable, independent work gets longer. The timing is much harder to predict.

r001.rationale: The response says replacement will happen “task by task” rather than in a single moment, and describes AI taking over well-defined tasks first.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize AI as concentrating power in a small number of people.

r003.rationale: It does not predict that most people will lose their distinctive value.

r004.rationale: It gives no estimate that roughly one-thousandth of today’s software engineering workforce could do all current work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it will happen task by task, rather than programmers suddenly disappearing. Writing code is only one part of programming. You also have to understand what someone wants, figure out how it fits into an existing system, and decide whether the result actually solves the problem.

When a task has a clear specification and a reliable way to test the answer, it’s much easier to automate. The harder cases are where the specification itself is unclear, or where a change has consequences that are difficult to verify. So I’d expect AI to take on increasingly complete tasks, while people spend more time defining problems, providing context, and evaluating results.

That could mean fewer people are needed for a particular project. But it could also mean we build software that previously wasn’t worth the cost. I’m uncertain about the overall effect on employment. The distinction I’d make is between replacing the act of writing code and replacing the person responsible for making the software useful. Those are different milestones.

r001.rationale: It says replacement will happen “task by task” rather than programmers suddenly disappearing, describing a gradual process.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize AI as concentrating power among a small number of people.

r003.rationale: It discusses changing programmer responsibilities but does not predict that most people will lose their distinctive value.

r004.rationale: It gives no estimate that roughly one-thousandth of the workforce could do all current software engineering work.
